body:
Meaning of a Digital Signature

A digital signature is a cryptographic mechanism used to verify the origin of digital information and help establish that the information has not been altered after signing.

A properly implemented digital signature can provide assurance of origin authenticity, data integrity and support for non-repudiation.

Non-repudiation means that the signature provides evidence connecting a signing operation to the holder of the relevant signing key. It does not eliminate every possible dispute about the person's identity or whether the private key was misused.

A digital signature is mainly used to verify authenticity and integrity. It does not automatically encrypt or conceal the contents of the signed document.

How Digital Signatures Work

Digital signatures commonly use asymmetric cryptography, involving a mathematically related public-key and private-key pair.

The signer uses the private signing key to produce a digital signature associated with the document. A recipient uses the corresponding public key to verify the signature.

If the signed document is changed after signing, a properly implemented verification process will ordinarily detect that the signed information no longer matches the signature.

The private signing key must be protected. The public verification key may be distributed to parties who need to verify signatures.

The Role of a Hash Function

A cryptographic hash function produces a fixed-length value derived from the contents of data. This value is often called a hash or message digest.

The hash acts like a compact digital fingerprint. If the contents of a document change, its cryptographic hash will ordinarily change as well.

Digital-signature systems commonly calculate a hash of a document and apply the signature operation to the hash rather than signing every part of the document individually.

A cryptographic hash is designed to be difficult to reverse. Unlike encryption, ordinary hashing does not provide a decryption process that restores the original document.

Hashing Is Not Encryption

FeatureEncryptionCryptographic hashing
Main purposeConceals information.Produces a fixed-length representation of information.
RecoveryAppropriate decryption can recover the original plaintext.No corresponding decryption operation recovers the original input.
Typical useProtecting confidentiality.Supporting integrity verification and digital signatures.

Comparing a document's hash with a trusted reference hash can help detect alteration. However, an ordinary hash value by itself does not prove who created the document. For that purpose, an authenticated reference or a suitable signature mechanism is needed.

Digital Signature Certificates

When verifying a signature, the recipient must also have reason to trust that the public verification key belongs to the claimed signer. A digital certificate helps establish an association between an identity and a public key.

In India, the Controller of Certifying Authorities (CCA) licenses and regulates Certifying Authorities under the Information Technology Act, 2000. Licensed Certifying Authorities (CAs) issue Digital Signature Certificates used in electronic authentication and digital-signature services.

These certificates help a recipient determine whether the public key used to verify a signature is associated with the claimed certificate holder. Reliable verification also depends on the validity of the certificate and the security of the associated private key.

Digital Signatures and Electronic Signatures

Electronic signature is a broader term for electronic methods of signing or authenticating records. A cryptographic digital signature is a particular type of electronic-signature mechanism.

A scanned image of a handwritten signature is not, merely by being placed inside a PDF, equivalent to a cryptographically verifiable digital signature.

India's eSign service allows users to apply legally recognised electronic signatures through an approved digital-signature process. The service uses identity authentication and digital-signature mechanisms supported by authorised service providers.

Digitally signed examination certificate

An institution digitally signs a certificate. The recipient verifies the signature using the appropriate public-key information and certificate. Successful verification helps establish that the signed record has not been altered and that the signature is associated with the claimed signing identity. The signature does not, by itself, prevent other people from reading the certificate.

Prelims focus

  • A digital signature supports authenticity, integrity and non-repudiation.
  • A private signing key is used to generate a digital signature.
  • The corresponding public key is used to verify it.
  • Cryptographic hashing produces a fixed-length message digest.
  • The Information Technology Act, 2000 provides India's legal framework for digital signatures.
  • The CCA licenses and regulates Certifying Authorities.
  • Trap: A digital signature does not automatically provide confidentiality.

[Sources: NIST Computer Security Resource Center Glossary, entries Digital Signature, Hash Function and Public Key, consulted 16 November 2026; Controller of Certifying Authorities, Government of India, About CCA and eSign: Online Electronic Signature Service, consulted 16 November 2026; Information Technology Act, 2000, section 3.]

pictures.caption: The private key creates a digital signature; the corresponding public key verifies it.

title: Digital Signatures, Hash Functions and Digital Certificates

body:
Why Secure Storage Is Necessary

Digital information may be stored on mobile phones, personal computers, office servers, removable storage devices and cloud services. Sensitive information can be disclosed through lost devices, compromised accounts, excessive sharing permissions or careless handling.

Protecting stored information therefore requires more than keeping the device physically safe. Appropriate safeguards must also control access to the information and reduce the consequences of theft, loss or misuse.

Basic Safeguards for Stored Data

1. Protect the Device and Account

Devices containing personal information should use suitable screen locks and authentication controls. Strong, unique passwords and multi-factor authentication provide additional protection for accounts where these controls are supported.

2. Use Encryption Where Appropriate

Device or file encryption can reduce unauthorised disclosure if a storage device is lost or copied. However, encryption is not a substitute for securing the account through which information is normally accessed.

3. Maintain Backups

A backup is a separate recoverable copy of information. Backups can help restore data after accidental deletion, device failure or certain cybersecurity incidents.

Backups should themselves be protected against unauthorised access. They should also be recoverable when the original information is unavailable.

4. Keep Systems Updated

Security updates can correct known weaknesses in operating systems and applications. Keeping devices and applications updated reduces exposure to threats that exploit outdated software.

5. Limit Access

Only users with a legitimate need should receive access to sensitive records. This is closely related to the principle of least privilege: a person or account should receive only the permissions necessary for its assigned task.

For example, a staff member who needs to inspect a document may require permission to read it but not permission to edit or delete it.

Sharing Information Securely

Secure sharing requires verifying the intended recipient and limiting the information and permissions provided. Encryption protects information during storage or transmission, but it does not decide whether the recipient is authorised to receive it.

Verify the Recipient

Before sending a confidential document, confirm the recipient's identity and contact details through a reliable channel. A mistyped email address or incorrect recipient selection may disclose the document even when the communication platform is secure.

Select Appropriate Sharing Permissions

Some file-sharing services allow access to named recipients, whereas others generate links that can be opened by anyone possessing the link. For confidential records, restricting access to specifically authorised recipients is generally safer than creating an unrestricted public link.

When supported, permissions should be limited to the necessary actions, such as viewing rather than editing. Access may also be restricted by an expiry date or withdrawn when no longer needed.

Share Only the Required Information

If an office needs a person's eligibility certificate, unrelated financial details should not be included merely because they happen to be stored in the same file. Unnecessary information may be omitted or appropriately redacted when permitted.

Recognise the Limits of Sharing Controls

Even a view-only document may sometimes be copied, photographed or reproduced by an authorised reader. Sharing restrictions reduce risk but cannot guarantee that information will never be redistributed.

Secure Sharing in Public Administration

Government departments handle records containing citizens' identity details, service applications, certificates and other personal information. These records should be shared according to legitimate administrative requirements rather than general convenience.

For example, when an office in Gujarat transfers an applicant's supporting documents to another authorised office, it should verify the receiving office, use an approved communication method and provide access only to the records necessary for the administrative task.

The same principles apply in education, banking, healthcare and other services. A secure communication method does not authorise unnecessary collection or disclosure.

Prelims focus

  • Encryption at rest protects stored information against certain unauthorised access risks.
  • Backups support recovery and availability.
  • Least privilege limits access to what is required for a task.
  • Recipient verification and restricted permissions reduce accidental disclosure.
  • Trap: Sending a file through an encrypted connection does not make an incorrect recipient authorised.

[Sources: Indian Computer Emergency Response Team, Cyber Security Best Practices for Senior Citizens, October 2025, Mobile Safety, Email Safety and Safe Browsing sections, pp. 2-3 and 8; NIST Computer Security Resource Center Glossary, entries Confidentiality, Authorisation and Availability, consulted 16 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Access permissions should be checked before sensitive records are shared.

title: Secure Storage and Sharing of Personal Information

body:
Meaning of Personal Data

Personal data is information relating to an identified or identifiable individual. A person's name, contact details, identification number or financial information may constitute personal data depending on the context.

Information does not have to contain a person's name to be personal data. Several pieces of information may identify an individual when considered together.

For example, a general statement about a district's population is not ordinarily personal data about a particular individual. However, a record linking a student's examination marks with a student identifier may be personal data because it concerns an identifiable person.

Digital personal data is personal data in digital form. It includes information originally collected digitally and information converted from physical records into digital form.

Meaning of Data Minimisation

Data minimisation means limiting the creation, collection, use, storage and disclosure of personal information to what is relevant and necessary for a legitimate, specified purpose.

This principle reduces unnecessary exposure of personal information. If less information is collected, there is generally less unnecessary information to protect, manage or potentially disclose.

Data minimisation requires collecting and processing only the personal data necessary for the intended purpose, rather than collecting additional information merely because it may be convenient or useful in the future.

Example: Online Education Application

Suppose an educational institution requires a student's name, contact details and relevant academic qualifications to process an admission application. Collecting these details may be justified by the application process.

Requesting access to the student's entire mobile contact list would ordinarily require a separate justification. The contact list is not automatically necessary simply because the student is using a mobile application.

The same principle applies to permissions requested by mobile applications. A service should not obtain unnecessary access to personal information merely because a device can technically provide it.

Data Minimisation Throughout the Information Life Cycle

Data minimisation is not limited to the moment of collection. Information should be handled responsibly throughout its use.

  1. Purpose: Identify the legitimate reason for collecting the information.
  2. Collection: Obtain only information relevant and necessary for that purpose.
  3. Use: Process the information for authorised purposes.
  4. Access and sharing: Limit disclosure to appropriate recipients and necessary information.
  5. Retention: Keep the information only as long as justified by the purpose and applicable legal requirements.
  6. Deletion or other disposal: When retention is no longer justified, remove or dispose of the information appropriately, subject to applicable legal obligations.

Privacy Safeguards for Citizens

Individuals can reduce unnecessary exposure of personal information through practical measures.

  • Provide personal information only when it is reasonably necessary for a genuine service or legally required process.
  • Review the purpose for which an application or website requests information.
  • Check app permissions and restrict unnecessary access to contacts, location or other personal information.
  • Use privacy settings to control the visibility of personal profiles and posts.
  • Avoid publicly posting identity documents, financial details or other sensitive information.
  • Use official services and verify unexpected requests before sharing personal details.
  • Review stored files and remove unnecessary copies when permitted.

Consent, Privacy and Security

Consent is a person's agreement to a particular use of information. Meaningful consent requires sufficient information about what is being requested and for what purpose. However, consent is not necessarily the only lawful basis for processing personal data; the applicable law may also recognise other legitimate grounds.

Privacy safeguards also include restricting access, protecting data from unauthorised disclosure, explaining relevant processing purposes and avoiding unnecessary retention.

An organisation might encrypt every personal record yet still violate the principle of data minimisation by collecting information unrelated to its service. Conversely, collecting only necessary information does not eliminate the need to protect it.

Security does not replace privacy

Encryption protects the confidentiality of information under appropriate conditions. It does not establish that the information was necessary to collect, that its use is authorised or that it may be retained indefinitely.

Data Minimisation Versus Data Security

Data minimisation and security are complementary. Minimisation reduces the amount and unnecessary exposure of information. Security controls protect the information that must legitimately be handled.

For example, an educational institution should avoid collecting unnecessary personal information and also protect the information that it does collect through appropriate access restrictions, authentication and storage safeguards.

Prelims focus

  • Personal data relates to an identified or identifiable individual.
  • Digital personal data is personal data in digital form.
  • Data minimisation limits processing to information necessary for a specified purpose.
  • Retention should be limited according to the purpose and applicable legal requirements.
  • Encryption and data minimisation address different aspects of protection.
  • Trap: Removing a name does not necessarily make information anonymous if the individual remains identifiable from other details.

[Sources: NIST Computer Security Resource Center Glossary, entry Minimization, consulted 16 November 2026; Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, section 2, definitions of personal data and digital personal data, and section 6(1), statutory statement of purpose-limited consent; Indian Computer Emergency Response Team, Cyber Security Best Practices for Senior Citizens, October 2025, Mobile Safety and Safe Browsing sections, pp. 2 and 8. The DPDP Act's substantive provisions have phased commencement, addressed in the following section.]

pictures.alt: Data minimisation applies at every stage: purpose, collection, use, access and sharing, retention, and appropriate disposal.
pictures.caption: Privacy protection begins before data collection and continues until appropriate disposal.

title: Data Minimisation, Personal Data and Practical Privacy Safeguards
